evidence.claim: across Rocky Mountain National Park

evidence.quote: Eleven miles of the route roam above tree line in the alpine tundra.

evidence.claim: Colorado’s transportation department highlights its cliffside engineering, overlooks and midsummer wildflowers, and lists two hours for the 48-mile drive.
evidence.quote: Length: 48 miles Driving time: 2 hours

evidence.claim: cliffside engineering
evidence.quote: this cliff-hugging highway is as impressive for its engineering

evidence.claim: Designated an All-American Road in 1996, Trail Ridge joins Beaver Meadow Road to form the longer byway between Grand Lake and Estes Park.
evidence.quote: Trail Ridge Road was designated by the U.S. Secretary of Transportation as an All-American Road, the highest level of designation, in 1996.

evidence.claim: Trail Ridge joins Beaver Meadow Road to form the longer byway between Grand Lake and Estes Park
evidence.quote: Together with the connecting 6.9-mile (11 km) Beaver Meadow Road (U.S. Highway 36), Trail Ridge Road forms the 55-mile (89 km) Trail Ridge Road/Beaver Meadow National Scenic Byway, an All-American Road.

evidence.claim: The earlier Fall River Road opened in 1921, but its single track, tight curves and grades reaching 16 percent proved inadequate for motor travel.
evidence.quote: Fall River Road was the first road into the park's high country. It opened in 1921 and quickly proved inadequate for motor travel as a single-track road with steep grades (up to 16%), tight curves and a short annual season due to snowpack.

evidence.claim: Construction of the new road began in 1929; by July 1932 it reached Fall River Pass with a maximum grade of 7 percent.
evidence.quote: Construction began in 1929 and was complete to Fall River Pass by July 1932, with a maximum grade of 7%.

evidence.claim: The connection through the Kawuneeche Valley to Grand Lake was completed in 1938.
evidence.quote: The road was complete through the Kawuneeche Valley to Grand Lake in 1938.

evidence.claim: Park Service design principles called for the new road to intrude as little as possible into the landscape.
evidence.quote: The road was designed to intrude as little as possible into the landscape, in accordance with Park Service design principles.

evidence.claim: Begin at Grand Lake and follow the North Fork of the Colorado River north through the Kawuneeche Valley.
evidence.quote: From Kawuneeche Visitor Center at the park's Grand Lake Entrance, Trail Ridge Road follows the North Fork of the Colorado River north through the Kawuneeche Valley.

evidence.claim: At Milner Pass, cross the Continental Divide beside Poudre Lake, then continue climbing past Fall River Pass and the Alpine Visitor Center.
evidence.quote: The pass provides the passage over the continental divide for  US 34, also known as Trail Ridge Road between Estes Park and Grand Lake.

evidence.claim: cross the Continental Divide beside Poudre Lake
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 34 passes the lake and crosses the Continental Divide at Milner Pass at the southwest end of the lake.

evidence.claim: continue climbing past Fall River Pass and the Alpine Visitor Center
evidence.quote: The Alpine Visitor Center, one of five visitor centers for Rocky Mountain National Park, is located at Fall River Pass.

evidence.claim: The road’s highest point lies farther east.
evidence.quote: the road does not descend after reaching the pass from the west, but instead continues to climb along a side ridge; thus, neither pass is the high point on Trail Ridge Road, which crests at 12,183 feet (3,713 m) elevation, east of Fall River Pass

evidence.claim: Follow Trail Ridge toward Deer Ridge Junction, then take the connecting Beaver Meadow Road toward the visitor center near Estes Park.
evidence.quote: The road follows Trail Ridge from the Fall River Pass near Alpine Visitor Center to the Deer Ridge Junction.

evidence.claim: take the connecting Beaver Meadow Road
evidence.quote: the connecting 6.9-mile (11 km) Beaver Meadow Road (U.S. Highway 36)

evidence.claim: the visitor center near Estes Park
evidence.quote: Beaver Meadows Visitor Center 1000 US Hwy 36 Estes Park, CO 80517

evidence.claim: Poudre Lake lies just east of the Continental Divide, beside the highway at Milner Pass.
evidence.quote: It is located just a few feet east of the Continental Divide in Larimer County, Colorado, United States. U.S. Route 34 passes the lake and crosses the Continental Divide at Milner Pass at the southwest end of the lake.

evidence.claim: The Cache la Poudre River flows from the lake; creeks on the other side of the pass lie near the Colorado River’s headwaters.
evidence.quote: The gentle pass divides the headwaters of the Cache la Poudre River (which issues from Poudre Lake just east of the pass) and several creeks near the headwaters of the Colorado River to the west.

evidence.claim: The crossing bears the name of T.J. Milner, an engineer who surveyed a possible railroad route here. That railway was never built.
evidence.quote: The pass is named in honor of T.J. Milner, an engineer who surveyed a potential railroad route over the pass. The railroad was never built.

evidence.claim: The road near the pass looks west toward the Never Summer Mountains.
evidence.quote: The road near the pass provides a panoramic view of the Never Summer Mountains to the west.

evidence.claim: Crossing the Divide does not finish the climb: Trail Ridge Road reaches its highest elevation, 12,183 feet, east of the pass.
evidence.quote: The pass is not, however, the high point on Trail Ridge Road, which crests at 12,183 ft (3,713 m) east of the pass

evidence.claim: Fall River Pass is high, but the highway keeps climbing east of it.
evidence.quote: the road does not descend after reaching the pass from the west, but instead continues to climb along a side ridge

evidence.claim: The Alpine Visitor Center stands at 11,796 feet, one mile west of Trail Ridge Road’s highest point.
evidence.quote: Rocky Mountain National Park's Alpine Visitor Center is located at 11,796 feet (3,595 m) above sea level at Fall River Pass, one mile west of the highest point on Trail Ridge Road

evidence.claim: It is the National Park System’s highest visitor center, with exhibits explaining the alpine tundra.
evidence.quote: It is the highest visitor center in the National Park System. The Alpine Visitor Center includes restrooms, exhibits on the alpine tundra ecosystem

evidence.claim: Views reach the Mummy Range and Fall River Valley to the east, and the Never Summer and Medicine Bow ranges to the west and north.
evidence.quote: Views from the Alpine Visitor Center include the Mummy Range, the Fall River Valley, and Trail Ridge to the east and the Never Summer and Medicine Bow ranges to the west and north.

evidence.claim: The quarter-mile round-trip Alpine Ridge Trail has acquired the name “Huffer’s Hill.”
evidence.quote: Hiking opportunities include the 1/4-mile round-trip Alpine Ridge Trail, commonly referred to as "Huffer's Hill,"

evidence.claim: Snow and the extreme winter environment limit the visitor center’s season; it opens around Memorial Day and closes around mid-October.
evidence.quote: The visitor center opens around Memorial Day and closes around mid-October due to snow and the extreme winter environment.

evidence.claim: The high road closes in winter and normally opens by Memorial Day weekend, weather permitting. Recorded road status: 970-586-1222.
evidence.quote: Normally opens by Memorial Day weekend, weather permitting.

evidence.claim: The high road closes in winter
evidence.quote: The higher portion of Trail Ridge Road is closed from October to May.

evidence.claim: Recorded road status: 970-586-1222.
evidence.quote: Recorded Trail Ridge Road status: (970) 586-1222

evidence.claim: From the visitor side, Beaver Meadows looks like a one-story building. The slope conceals a second level.
evidence.quote: As seen from visitor (north) side, the building presents as a single-story structure, but is actually two stories owing to the sloping terrain on which it is built.

evidence.claim: Taliesin Associated Architects designed it after Frank Lloyd Wright’s death, and construction finished in 1967.
evidence.quote: Completed in 1967, it was designed by Taliesin Associated Architects, and was one of the most significant commissions for that firm in the years immediately following the death of founder Frank Lloyd Wright.

evidence.claim: It was among the last major projects of Mission 66, the National Park Service’s program to renew its parks.
evidence.quote: As part of the Park Service's Mission 66 program to revitalize the nation's park system

evidence.claim: among the last major projects of Mission 66
evidence.quote: It was also one of the last major projects completed under the Park Service Mission 66 project.

evidence.claim: Sandstone slabs are embedded in cast concrete panels, with a steel frame supporting the building.
evidence.quote: It is a rectangular structure, built with a steel frame and cast concrete panels, into which slabs of sandstone have been embedded.

evidence.claim: A Snogo snowplow is displayed at the center.
evidence.quote: A Snogo Snow Plow is on display at the center.

evidence.claim: The eastern end serves visitors, while park offices occupy the western end, where movable partitions allow the interior layout to change.
evidence.quote: The building's eastern end is devoted to visitor facilities

evidence.claim: park offices occupy the western end, where movable partitions allow the interior layout to change
evidence.quote: The western end houses park offices in a modular design with movable partitions.

evidence.claim: Sandstone slabs are embedded in the building’s cast concrete panels.
evidence.quote: cast concrete panels, into which slabs of sandstone have been embedded.
